englishCandidates.title: Beyond the pale
englishCandidates.meaning:
Outside the bounds of morality, acceptable behavior or good judgement, etc.

# Example
"He was so rude at that party. His behavior was beyond the pale"

# Etymology
From pale (“jurisdiction of an authority, territory under an authority's jurisdiction”), suggesting that anything outside the authority's jurisdiction was uncivilized. The phrase was in use by the mid-17th century, and may be a reference to the general sense of boundary, but is often understood to refer specifically to the English Pale in Ireland. In the nominally English territory of Ireland, only the Pale fell genuinely under the authority of English law, hence the terms within the pale and beyond the pale. The boundary of the Ashdown Forest (a royal hunting forest) was also known as the Pale, consisting of a paled fence and a ditch inside, to allow deer to jump in, but not back out.

englishCandidates.title: Cutting off one's nose to spite one's face
englishCandidates.normalizedTitle: cutting off one s nose to spite one s face
englishCandidates.meaning:
"Cutting off one's nose to spite one's face" is an expression used to describe a needlessly self-destructive overreaction to a problem: "Don't cut off your nose to spite your face" is a warning against acting out of pique, or against pursuing revenge in a way that would damage oneself more than the object of one's anger.

# Variations
- Cut off your nose to spite your face

# Etymology
It was not uncommon in the Middle Ages for a person to cut off the nose of another for various reasons, including punishment from the state, or as an act of revenge.

The expression has since become a blanket term for (often unwise) self-destructive actions motivated purely by anger or desire for revenge. For example, if a man was angered by his wife, he might burn down their house to punish her; however, burning down her house would also mean burning down his, along with all of their possessions.

In the 1796 edition of Francis Grose's Classical Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue, "He cut off his nose to be revenged of his face" is said to apply to "one who, to be revenged on his neighbor, has materially injured himself."

In contradistinction to the above, Saint Ebbe, Abbess of Coldingham Priory in south-east Scotland, and her nuns, who are reported to have severed their own noses and upper lips, were not motivated by anger or revenge, but desperately tried to save their integrity by grossly disfiguring themselves to the point of becoming unattractive as targets of rape to the invading Viking raiders.

englishCandidates.title: What's good for the goose is good for the gander
englishCandidates.normalizedTitle: what s good for the goose is good for the gander
englishCandidates.meaning:
If something is good for one person, it should be equally as good for another person; someone who treats another in a certain way should not complain if the same is done to them.

# Etymology
From the earlier expression `From earlier what's sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander`. In 1670s, figuratively using goose/gander for women and men, and literally meaning that the same sauce applies equally well to cooked goose, regardless of sex. Early forms include `as deep drinketh the goose as the gander` and similar `As well for the coowe calfe as for the bull` (1549). The expression appears in Dickens when a spy attempting to evade culpability insists,`For you cannot sarse the goose and not the gander.`

englishCandidates.title: Wild goose chase
englishCandidates.meaning:
A futile search, a fruitless errand; a useless and often lengthy task whose execution is inordinately complex relative to the value of the outcome. 

# Etymology
Early recorded use refers to a type of 16th century horse race where everyone had to try to follow the erratic course of the lead horse, like wild geese have to follow their leader in formation. Mentioned in 1593 in the English poet Gervase Markham’s book about horsemanship. Also mentioned in the William Shakespeare play Romeo and Juliet, Act 2, scene 4 by the character Mercutio: "Nay, if our wits run the wild-goose chase, I am done; for thou hast more of the wild goose in one of thy wits than, I am sure, I have in my whole five." Mentioned in Robert Burton, Anatomy of Melancholy (1621). Common use in the current may be the origin for the sport sense.[1]

# Sources

englishCandidates.title: world's smallest violin
englishCandidates.meaning:
A notional violin that plays tragic music for the afflicted; used in dismissive responses to complaints of woe.


# Etymology
A version of Hearts and Flowers on violin was used in many melodramatic films in the early 1900s. From this and the use of other violin pieces in melodramatic films derive the term hearts and flowers (“extremely sentimental and sweet”), the phrase break out the violins (in a dismissive/sarcastic show of sympathy), and the image of a violin (small, to reflect that the woe complained of is perceived to be small) playing Hearts and Flowers or "the world's saddest song" in response to complaints of woe.

mappings.meaning: Conviene conservar una situación conocida y segura, aunque sea imperfecta, antes que arriesgarla por otra aparentemente mejor pero incierta.
mappings.literalTranslation: The known bad is worth more than the good yet to be known.
mappings.usageNotes: Refrán de uso actual en España. Funciona como equivalente pragmático, aunque pone el acento en preferir lo familiar, incluso si es malo, frente a una alternativa desconocida; el inglés enfatiza más directamente una ganancia segura frente a otra potencialmente mayor. También se usa con artículos: «Más vale lo malo conocido que lo bueno por conocer».

sources.title: Más vale malo conocido que bueno por conocer

sources.title: Más vale un 'toma' que dos 'te daré'
sources.excerpt: «Felides. ¡Oh, Pandulfo!, mucho te agradezco tu buena diligencia [...] yo te prometo que yo te lo satisfaga si llevas a fin estos hechos. Pandulfo. No querría yo que fuesse todo parolas, porque más quiero un toma que dos te daré»
sources.attestedForm: más quiero un toma que dos te daré
sources.supports: La respuesta contrapone una recompensa tangible a una promesa futura y posiblemente incumplida. La misma ficha define el refrán como preferencia por lo que se tiene en el presente frente a algo mejor pero futuro e incierto.

sources.title: Diálogo secular
sources.excerpt: El XIX.- Escarmienta en mí, hijo mío; cumple lo que ofrezcas, que prometer y no dar hace a los tontos alegrar. El XX.- No seré yo quien falte a mis compromisos. Pienso ofrecer poco, que más vale un toma que dos te daré.
sources.attestedForm: más vale un toma que dos te daré

mappings.title: Mieux vaut tenir que courir
mappings.meaning: Il est préférable de conserver ou de saisir un avantage certain plutôt que de poursuivre un gain supérieur mais incertain.
mappings.literalTranslation: Better to hold than to run after [something].
mappings.usageNotes: Proverbe français bien attesté, parfois employé sous la forme « Il vaut mieux tenir que courir ». Il correspond directement au sens pragmatique de l’idiome anglais : privilégier ce que l’on possède ou peut obtenir sûrement plutôt qu’une perspective plus avantageuse mais aléatoire. Son registre est proverbial et quelque peu traditionnel, mais il reste intelligible en France.

sources.supports: Dans ce roman de Maurice Level, un policier invoque le proverbe pour recommander de sécuriser immédiatement le suspect qu’il croit tenir plutôt que de différer l’arrestation et risquer de le perdre.

sources.title: Les Habits noirs, partie 3, chapitre XI

mappings.title: Meglio un uovo oggi che una gallina domani
mappings.meaning: È preferibile un vantaggio piccolo ma sicuro e immediato a un vantaggio maggiore che potrebbe arrivare in futuro ma rimane incerto.
mappings.literalTranslation: Better an egg today than a hen tomorrow.
mappings.usageNotes: Proverbio italiano naturale, comune e semanticamente equivalente a “A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush”. La forma canonica è “Meglio un uovo oggi che una gallina domani”; nell’uso giornalistico ricorrono anche la variante interrogativa “meglio l’uovo oggi o la gallina domani?” e richiami abbreviati come “l’uovo oggi” contrapposto alla “gallina domani”. Può raccomandare prudenza, ma viene anche impiegato per discutere criticamente la preferenza per una ricompensa immediata.
